# Decision Trees for Classification

::: {.callout-note title="Connection with the theoretical volume"}
The mathematical treatment of entropy, impurity, recursive partitions, and decision trees is developed in Chapters 3, 6, and 13 of *Mathematical Foundations of Machine Learning* [@rodriguez2026fundamentos].
:::

## Learning objectives

By the end of this chapter, the reader will be able to explain how a classification tree partitions predictor space, interpret the Gini index, train a controlled tree in R, assess its complexity, and evaluate its predictions on held-out data.

## Basic idea

A decision tree classifies observations through a sequence of if-then rules. At each internal node, the algorithm selects a variable and a split that reduce class impurity.

A common impurity measure is the Gini index:

$$
Gini = 1-\sum_{k=1}^{K}p_k^2.
$$

A pure node has low impurity because most of its observations belong to the same class.

## Controlling tree complexity

A tree can fit training data extremely well and still generalize poorly. Parameters such as complexity cost, minimum split size, minimum terminal-node size, and maximum depth limit unnecessary growth.

::: {.callout-important title="Interpretability does not eliminate overfitting"}
A tree may be easy to explain and still be statistically unstable. Interpretability and generalization are different properties and both must be evaluated.
:::

## ATUS example

The Spanish edition uses `rpart` to classify accidents as **with victims** or **property damage only**, using month, hour, day of week, accident type, and cause. The data are split into training and test sets before fitting the tree.

The resulting confusion matrix is summarized with accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity.

## Variable importance

Tree importance scores describe how strongly predictors contributed to splits in the fitted tree. They are useful for describing the model but should not be interpreted as causal effects.

::: {.callout-warning title="Association is not causation"}
A variable can be highly useful for prediction without being a cause of the outcome. Tree-based importance reflects predictive contribution inside the fitted model.
:::

## COVID-19 educational route

The COVID-19 case uses the same predictor set introduced in previous chapters. The processed data file is selected dynamically so that the chapter does not depend on a hard-coded calendar year.

```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(rpart)

files_covid <- list.files(
  "../datos/covid19/procesados",
  pattern = "covid19_mexico_[0-9]{4}_ml_preparado\\.csv\\.gz$",
  full.names = TRUE
)

if (length(files_covid) == 0) {
  stop("No prepared COVID-19 data file was found.")
}

covid_tree <- read_csv(files_covid[1], show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  select(
    MURIO, EDAD, NEUMONIA, DIABETES, HIPERTENSION,
    OBESIDAD, RENAL_CRONICA, NUM_COMORBILIDADES
  ) |>
  drop_na()
```

A controlled tree can then be fitted to a training subset with `rpart(method = "class")` and evaluated on the test subset.

::: {.callout-warning title="Educational use only"}
Rules found in this sample describe patterns in the selected data. They must not be interpreted as clinical decision rules or medical recommendations.
:::

## Pruning and validation

The complexity table produced by `printcp()` helps study the trade-off between tree size and error. Final pruning or hyperparameter selection should be based on validation or cross-validation, leaving the final test set untouched until the end.

## Chapter summary

Decision trees translate classification into understandable recursive rules. Their strengths are interpretability and flexibility; their weaknesses include instability and susceptibility to overfitting. Complexity control and out-of-sample evaluation are therefore essential.
